data.title: Wogastisburg – the most important hillfort of Samo's Empire
data.excerpt: Fredegar's Chronicle records how the Franks of Dagobert I laid siege to the hillfort of Wogastisburg and, after three days of fighting, fled, leaving behind all their tents and baggage. Where the most important hillfort of Samo's Empire stood is still unknown: historians have placed it in Bohemia, in Moravia, in Carinthia, in the Danube valley of north-eastern Austria, and at Bratislava or Devín.
data.metaTitle: Wogastisburg: the hillfort where Samo defeated Dagobert
data.metaDescription: In Fredegar's Chronicle, Samo's Slavs routed Dagobert's Frankish army here in a three-day battle. But where did the enigmatic Wogastisburg actually lie?

timeline.title: A second generation comes of age and a revolt is prepared
timeline.description: In Pannonia a second generation of Avar–Slavic offspring had grown up, and they were preparing a revolt against Avar oppression.

timeline.title: The arrival of the merchant Samo
timeline.description: A merchant caravan led by Samo “from the Senonian country” appeared on the Middle Danube; he helped the Slavs in their revolt and they chose him as their ruler.

timeline.title: The rise of Samo's Empire
timeline.description: The first empire of the Slavs came into being beyond the Danube, in the territory of south-western Slovakia, southern Moravia, north-eastern Austria and part of the Czech lands.

timeline.title: Battles against the Avars and release from their rule
timeline.description: Under Samo's leadership the Slavs “pacified” the Avars in several battles and freed themselves from their rule; the first Slavic principalities arose.

timeline.title: Relations with the Frankish Empire deteriorate
timeline.description: After the alliance with Prince Dervan and the raids into Thuringia, relations with the Franks soured; the envoy Sicharius came to Samo's court.

timeline.title: The famous battle of Wogastisburg
timeline.description: The central battle against the Franks, at which the core of the Slavic war forces was concentrated. The text gives no specific year for it; chronologically it fits the conflict with the Franks after 630.

timeline.title: Samo's death and the collapse of the empire
timeline.description: After the ruler's death the empire fell apart; Great Moravia later built on its foundations.

blocks.text: Then, when the Austrasians laid siege to the fortress of Wogastisburg, where very numerous companies of the valiant Wends (the Slavs) had fortified themselves, many of Dagobert's army (the Frankish king) were there put to the sword in a three-day battle, and the rest, abandoning all the tents and baggage they had, returned thence in cowardice to their own dwellings. Thereafter the Wends burst into Thuringia and into the other regions of the Frankish Empire several times and plundered. Even Dervan, prince of the race of the Sorbs, who were of the tribe of the Slavs and had long belonged to the Frankish Empire, joined themselves with them to the ruler Samo.
blocks.author: Fredegar's Chronicle

children.text: Wogastisburg and Samo's Empire

If you ask most Slovaks what Wogastisburg was, you will be as unpleasantly surprised as I was by how many of them will not have the faintest idea. The aim of this article is therefore to acquaint readers with this exceptionally important Slavic hillfort and with the glorious moments of the first empire of the Slavs — Samo's Empire. Samo's Empire existed from 623 and evidently came to an end after the death of its ruler — that is, after 658. Samo was the first ruler to unite the Slavs to such a degree that they freed themselves from the power of the hegemon of the day — the Avars — and also won complete independence from the mightiest state of that time — the Frankish Empire. These glorious times are recorded fairly credibly, and in detail by the standards of the period, by an important source — Fredegar's Chronicle.
Let us therefore allow the medieval chronicler to go on telling of the events that took place in his own time and that are of such great importance for Slovak history:

blocks.text: In the fortieth year of Chlothar's reign a man named Samo, a Frank by birth from the Senonian country, brought many merchants with him and set out to trade with the Slavs who are nicknamed Wends. The Slavs had already begun to rise against the Avars, who are called Huns, and against their ruler, the khagan. The Wends had long been the vanguard (the double line – the double regiment) of the Huns; when the Huns led an attack with their army against any tribe whatsoever, the Huns drew up their assembled host in defence of the camps, while the Wends did the fighting. If victory inclined to their side, the Huns then attacked in order to seize the spoils, but if the Wends were being beaten, they gathered strength again, supported by the auxiliary army of the Huns. The Huns therefore called them the vanguard, because at a battle encounter they formed double battle lines and marched ahead of the Huns. Every year the Huns came to the Slavs to spend the winter, and took the wives of the Slavs and their daughters to their beds. Besides the other acts of violence (which they endured:), the Slavs paid tribute to the Huns. The sons of the Huns, whom they had begotten by the wives of the Wends and (:their:) daughters, no longer endured the evil of cruelty and violence, resisted the rule of the Huns and, as I have already mentioned, began to rebel. When the Wends attacked the Huns with an army, the merchant Samo, whom I have likewise mentioned, advanced with them in the host. And there he showed such great ability against the Huns that it aroused admiration, and an immense number of them was put to the sword by the Wends. The Wends, recognising Samo's usefulness, chose him as king over themselves, and there he reigned happily for 35 years. During his reign the Wends fought many battles against the Huns. With his prudence and ability the Wends always defeated the Huns. Samo had 12 wives of the tribe of the Wends, by whom he begot 22 sons and 15 daughters.
blocks.author: Fredegar's Chronicle

children.text: A comment on the chronicle entry:

"Around 620, according to J. Steinhübel, a second generation of Avar–Slavic offspring had already grown up in Pannonia. It was precisely there that the revolt against Avar oppression, which they had been preparing, broke out. It was some time in the summer of 622 when a merchant caravan led by the merchant Samo "from the Senonian country" appeared in the region of the Middle Danube. He helped the Slavs in the revolt, above all by offering military services. He proved to be a good organiser, and so the Slavs chose him as their ruler. There followed several battles in 623–624, when under his leadership they "pacified" the Avars and freed themselves from their rule. In the time of these anti-Avar revolts and battles the first Slavic principalities arose — the Croatian, the Slavonian and the Carinthian.

children.text: Subsequently, according to J. Steinhübel, after the outbreak of the revolt the tribes of the Wends, the Croats, the Sorbs and in part also the Dudlebi left Pannonia and occupied the area neighbouring this troubled region. Beyond the Danube, that is, in the territory of south-western Slovakia, southern Moravia and probably also north-eastern Austria and part of the Czech lands, they founded a Slavic "empire". Thus the so-called Samo's Empire enters history." (http://dubrava.vkrp.sk)

blocks.text: In that year the Slavs, called Wends, in Samo's realm killed a great number of Frankish merchants and robbed them of their goods. This was the beginning of the quarrel between Dagobert and Samo, the ruler of the Slavs. And Dagobert sent the envoy Sycharius to Samo with the request that he give due compensation for the merchants whom his (;people:) had killed, or for the goods they had unlawfully appropriated. Samo did not wish to see Sycharius, nor would he have allowed him to (:come:) before him. Sycharius (:therefore:), dressed in clothing in the manner of the Slavs, came with his men before Samo's sight; he announced to him everything that had been entrusted to him. But as is the (:custom:) of paganism and of the arrogance of the ignoble, Samo gave no compensation for what his (:people:) had committed; he wished only to arrange negotiations, so that in the matter of these and other complaints which had arisen between the parties justice might be mutually satisfied. Sycharius, like a foolish envoy, spoke rash words to Samo which had not been entrusted to him, and even threats, that Samo and the people of his realm were supposedly bound in service to Dagobert. Samo, by now offended, said in reply: “Both the land we hold belongs to Dagobert and we too belong to him, if, that is, he orders friendship to be kept with us.” Sycharius answered: “It is not possible for Christians and servants of God to make friendship with dogs.” To this Samo said: “If you are servants of God and we are God's dogs, then since you act continually against him, we have taken leave to tear you apart with our teeth.” Sycharius was driven away from before Samo's eyes. When he reported this to Dagobert, Dagobert arrogantly ordered that the army of the whole Austrasian realm should march against Samo and the Wends. When the army attacked the Wends drawn up in three divisions, the Lombards too, bribed by Dagobert, likewise advanced in hostility against the Slavs. The Slavs in these and in other places were making (:military:) preparations against this; whichever region the army of the Alemanni under the duke Chrodobert set foot in, it was victorious. The Lombards likewise were victorious, and both the Alemanni and the Lombards carried off with them a very great number of captives from among the Slavs. Then, when the Austrasians laid siege to the fortress of Wogastisburg, where very numerous companies of the valiant Wends had fortified themselves, many of Dagobert's army were there put to the sword in a three-day battle, and the rest, abandoning all the tents and baggage they had, returned thence in cowardice to their own dwellings. Thereafter the Wends burst into Thuringia and into the other regions of the Frankish Empire several times and plundered. Even Dervan, prince of the race of the Sorbs, who were of the tribe of the Slavs and had long belonged to the Frankish Empire, joined themselves with them to the ruler Samo. This victory which the Wends won over the Franks was helped not so much by the valour of the Slavs as by the folly of the Austrasians, who had meanwhile realised that they had fallen into Dagobert's hatred and that they would be plundered continually.

children.text: A comment on the chronicle entry: "So after the rise of this "empire" the Frankish king Dagobert I, of the Merovingian dynasty, at first welcomed the existence of a Slavic power formation beyond his eastern frontier. It served to protect his territory against the warlike Avars. After 630, however, mutual relations deteriorated, after Samo's Slavs had concluded an alliance with the Elbe Sorbian prince Dervan and were making devastating raids into the Thuringia region. The Frankish envoy Sicharius therefore came to Samo's court, where he was to mediate a new agreement. He accused the Slavs of stealing the goods of a Frankish merchant caravan and of murdering Frankish merchants. As we can see, some things do not change, and pretexts for starting a war in particular tend to be particularly transparent, the earliest times not excepted." (http://dubrava.vkrp.sk)

blocks.text: In the eleventh year of Dagobert's reign, when the Wends on Samo's orders boldly committed atrocities and ever more often, crossing their borders to plunder the Frankish Empire, attacked Thuringia and the other regions, Dagobert came to the city of Metz and, on the advice of the bishops as well as of the church dignitaries and with the consent of all the magnates of his realm, raised his son Sigybert to be king of Austrasia and allowed him to have the city of Metz as his seat. Chunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne, and the prince Adalgysel were appointed commander of the court, so that he might govern the realm. He handed over to his son a treasure that was sufficient and, fittingly as was proper, set (him) at its head. He ordained that everything he had granted him should be separately confirmed in written decrees. Then of their own accord they resolved jointly to defend the frontier and the Frankish Empire against the Wends...
blocks.author: Fredegar's Chronicle

children.text: Samo's Empire — that is great glory and a great event in the history of the Slavic world. Not only did the Slavs present themselves in such a light on the stage of European history for the first time, but in the encounter of two worlds they managed to win their independence bravely. Even the allied European armies came to grief against them. Let us not be surprised, then, that as soon as Fredegar's Chronicle was discovered, every Slavic nation took an eager interest in the fate of this first tentative Slavic state. For Samo's Empire was shrouded in a veil of unanswered questions.
Where did Wogastisburg stand?

blocks.alt: Wogastisburg – the most important hillfort of Samo's Empire

children.text: Where, then, did that famous hillfort (or a “burgus”?) which the chronicler calls by the name Wogastisburg actually lie? No one is likely to provide conclusive proof of that any more; indeed, if such proof were found, it would be the discovery of the century. Among historians of various countries we of course see an effort to “appropriate” Wogastisburg and to claim that this or that site in their own country was unambiguously Wogastisburg. The hillfort has been placed in Bohemia, in Moravia, in Carinthia and, of course — so that we Slovaks are not left out either — several of our historians can imagine that this hillfort was Bratislava, or Devín. I myself have no objection to this effort and am of the opinion that it is better to look for reasons why it should be so than for reasons why it should not — for the latter we have historians enough from other countries.
A very interesting article on precisely this subject can be found at http://www.svatohaj.sk/samovarisa.html, and I take the liberty of quoting it:

Fredegar's Chronicle is the only trustworthy historical source of information about Samo and his kingdom. There is a second source: On the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians (the Conversio), but it was written two hundred years later and is not entirely trustworthy. It drew on the sparse records known under the name Gesta Dagoberti regis – made from Fredegar's Chronicle – which were an equally tendentious work. From this source arose the error which the Romantics used against German slander, claiming that Samo was a Slav by origin. German historians, by contrast, promoted the idea that he was a Germanic man by origin. From the analysis of the Old Celtic dictionary by A. Holder, however, it is clear that the name Samo is of Celtic origin. And where did Samo come from? The Senonian country lay near the present-day town of Sens in France and is today known under the name Champagne. It was a region in which all the important roads crossed, including those running east – into the Danube basin. In this region the Celtic pagan tradition survived in the mountainous parts even in the sixth century. Samo was therefore a Celt by origin, a subject of the Frankish Empire, but above all he was a trader. A trader who, like many others, decided to make money out of a war. Out of the dispute between the Slavs and the Avars. The Slavs needed good weapons in order to offset the military superiority of the Avars, and that was an opportune moment for trade. Samo gathered many merchants and at the head of this armed caravan set out for the territory of the Slavs. The merchant companies of those days saw to their own protection, so it is very likely that the merchants themselves were skilled in the art of war, which Fredegar's Chronicle also confirms to us about Samo.

There were long disputes about where it was that Samo actually came to. Historians looked for the core of Samo's Empire (I am rather in favour of the name kingdom) in Bohemia, in eastern Germany and in Carinthia. The views advocating Carinthia as the territory of Samo's kingdom quickly dissolved once it was established that the Conversio is not a trustworthy source. The Carinthian Slavs were too dependent on the Lombards, and we would surely have learned of their revolt from their own history. Fredegar's Chronicle also mentions that later they made raids into Thuringia as well, and Carinthia would hardly have been a suitable place from which to attack the Frankish Empire, because the territory of the Avars separated it; from Carinthia it would have been far better to attack Bavaria. Archaeology has unambiguously refuted Bohemia and Germany as the territory of Samo's rule. For there were never any Avars in these territories, nor in the neighbouring areas, and so these Slavs could not have risen against them. The north-western extent of the Avars ended roughly in the territory of present-day Hungary. In the north, then, it reached as far as the Danube and to the south of the Košice Basin, and in the west as far as the river Leitha near the eastern Austrian border. Samo's Empire must therefore have lain somewhere along this frontier, and the most numerous occupation of this period has been uncovered by archaeology in the Bratislava area. Many Avar–Slavic cemeteries have been found here, from which we can observe that the Slavs had a numerical preponderance in this territory and were free, because they bore arms. This territory also lies on the old trade route running from Spain through France to Germany and along the Danube further east as far as the Orient. Moreover, this route crosses here with the well-known Amber Road, which runs as far as the eastern Baltic coast.

This, then, is in all probability where the core of Samo's kingdom or empire lay. How far it extended we can only guess, but it is quite possible that it reached the territory of Bohemia, since the prince of the Lusatian Sorbs, Dervan, also joined Samo's Empire. Here at the Bratislava Gate, at the well-guarded fords across the Danube, the famous battles against the Avar tribes were fought. In Fredegar's Chronicle we find a mention that the Avars came to the Slavs to spend the winter. This was because the Avars were not used to storing hay for their horses for the winter. They were excellent riders who could shoot accurately at a gallop and wield a sabre or a war axe. They were at home in metallurgy, but not in agriculture. In battle they made full use of the advantages of cavalry – speed of movement. They were literally grown together with their horses, and their physiognomy was adapted to this as well. They had short, O-shaped legs and stunted feet. The shape of their heads was typically Asiatic – a flattened face and black hair. But the Slavs were no doves either. The records from Byzantium that praise Slavic warriors for their scouting skills bear witness to this. The Slavs were excellent at camouflaging themselves in the woods, at ambushing from cover, at fighting in ravines and marshes and at setting traps.

If Samo's Empire was to come into being at all, however, the Slavs living here had to reach a level of husbandry that allowed them to support a non-productive apparatus of soldiers and leaders. Not least, they had to overcome tribal fragmentation, and a foreigner could serve them excellently for that. Many cases are known from history in which the ambitions of individual chieftains did not allow any one of them to take power, and so it was precisely a man from abroad, whom all of them could accept, who took over as ruler. It is also possible that Samo did not come to an entirely foreign country. It is likely that even in his day assimilated remnants of the Celtic Cotini, who had survived in the ore-bearing mountains, still lived here. Samo quickly settled in here and adopted Slavic customs and ways, among them polygamy. During his reign (623 – 658) the Slavs fought many battles against the Avars and won every time; later they even turned, together with their ruler – originally a Frankish subject – against the Frankish Empire and achieved no small successes in that struggle. After his death the empire did indeed fall apart, but Great Moravia evidently built on its foundations later on."

One can agree with many of the author's opinions — for example, the statement at the end of the article that Great Moravia was built on the remains of Samo's Empire is very likely. In some places, such as Nitra, Devín, Mikulčice and so on, the continuity of the rule of regional magnates from the time of Samo's Empire could doubtless have been preserved, even if they evidently did not act in unison as part of a single empire. In the decades that followed the collapse there were probably power struggles and efforts at unification, which continued with the rise of the Principality of Nitra and of the Moravian principality and culminated in the defeat of Pribina and the creation of Great Moravia.

An interesting (though I do not claim a certainly correct) explanation of the name Wogastisburg was also offered by Matúš Kučera in the book Slovensko v dobách stredovekých (Slovakia in the Middle Ages), where he writes:

Let us look first at the little word burc (burg). Everyone has somehow taken it for granted that even in Fredegar's day it meant what it later meant in the German language — a solid masonry castle. At that time, however, such castles did not yet exist. Nor have archaeologists so far managed to find in the territory of present-day Slovakia even hillforts fortified with earthen ramparts. Our ancestors did not yet build such things in the 6th and at the beginning of the 7th century; somehow they did not need them.

On further and deeper investigation it was found that the little word really is of Germanic origin, but that it had been borrowed before the Slavs already by the Romans, who gave it a peculiar, unique content. They used it to name fortress towers, but also the large fortress complexes which they built on the frontier between their own empire and the barbarian Germanic world. The fortified frontier ran along the Danube, which was itself a barrier difficult to overcome for the people of deep antiquity and of the early Middle Ages, and it was called the Limes romanus. Along its whole length the Romans built many burgs or burguses. From present-day Budapest through Komárno as far as Bratislava alone, for example, more than forty of them towered above the Danubian plain. Some were only small watchtowers, but at places where a great and busy road crossed the Limes, or where the Danube could be forded even with a carter's wagon (for example near present-day Bratislava), large and sprawling fortified places — burgs — grew up. (In present-day England, where such burgs have survived well, we know of some with an area of as much as 20 hectares, and the English call them burghs to this day.) They were in fact marketplaces where Roman and barbarian merchants met and exchanged and sold goods to one another. There were several such merchant burgs on the Danubian limes line. And that they were indeed well chosen and long known is attested by the names of many towns in which the little word burg has remained. We know Strasbourg, Augsburg, Regensburg, Salzburg and other names. There is one in the territory of present-day Slovakia too, namely the old name of our Bratislava. From the Slavic prince Braslav, who had his seat in the hillfort on the present-day castle hill, the name Braslavs-burg (that is, Braslav's burg) was formed, from it Brrslavsburg and further Pressburg, from which it is only a small step to the familiar Prešporok. The old name of Bratislava thus reminds us that a burg in which merchants met and traded extended over the area of the present-day city as well. And since we also know that merchants were once called gast or gost (from which our word hosť, a guest, arose), we have come very close indeed to the explanation of the mysterious Wogastisburg. It was undoubtedly a burg where merchants — gosti — had met since time immemorial. Such a place was most certainly visited by the merchant Samo too when he travelled to the Slavic lands, just as it is certain that he did not wander about mountains and hills but went nicely along the old Roman road through the Danube basin. That is why we must look for the Burgus of guests, Wo-gastis-burg, by this mighty river."
(Matúš Kučera: Slovensko v dobách stredovekých, Mladé letá 1985)
A few further views on the location of Wogastisburg:

"The oldest view attempting to clarify the position of this hillfort places it in the Main region, through which the royal road of the Frankish war expeditions to the east ran. What is more, we encounter here a site which to this day bears the name "Wogastesrode". This theory is further supported by the existence of the aforementioned alliance with the Sorbian Dervan, which points to a considerable extent of the "empire" towards the west. A crack in this thesis is, however, introduced by the fact that no Old Slavic hillfort of the 7th century has been discovered in this area. Moreover, it is questionable whether a hillfort so important that the core of the Slavic war forces was concentrated at it would have lain so far to the west, in territory under direct Frankish influence — and that even if we accept the idea that it was a "frontier" fortress.

Other voices, in turn, point out that "Vogasgrad" should rather be sought in the centre of the empire, where we have both hillforts of this period attested archaeologically and the Avar–Slavic society which, according to the Frankish chronicles, is supposed to have taken part in the creation and the functioning of the empire. Here the area of the Devín Gate at the confluence of the Morava and the Danube comes into consideration. But here again there is the problem of the absence of any find of a hillfort of this period. The assumed position in the area of southern Moravia already appears more tenable, as the hillforts mentioned above theoretically meet the "requirements" of the sought-after Vogastisburg. Direct evidence, however, is still lacking.

A view was also expressed at one time placing it in north-eastern Austria, in the Danube valley. There may be something in that, since we know that the Carinthian Slavs too were, with great probability, Samo's allies for a time."

The historian Anton Hrnko, in the article Devín – božská perla Slovenska (Devín – the divine pearl of Slovakia) on the website http://www.hrnko.sk/category/slovenske-dejiny/page/5/, says the following about the location of Wogastisburg:

"The old Roman fortress at the mouth of the river Enns into the Danube in the little town of Albing best meets all the criteria. Of the many fortified places on the Roman Limes, there are few whose ancient name has not survived. The fortress at Albing is among them. In reconstructing its name these historians start from the frequent Roman practice of naming the towns on the Limes not after the rivers on which they lay beside the Danube, but after the rivers that flowed into the Danube opposite them (for example Regensburg (Rezno) – the river Regen; Passau (Pasov) – the river Boiodurum, today's Ilz). Even the German name of Esztergom is identical with the name of the river Hron, which flows into the Danube opposite it (Gran). Since the river opposite Albing (today's Aist) was called Agasta in antiquity, they conclude that the fortress on the boundary between the Frankish and the Slavic sphere of power was also called Agasta, from which the Germanic name Wogastisburg could logically have arisen (just as somewhat later the German name Breslawasburg, Pressburg, arose from the Slovak Bräslava).

From the argument set out above, which in my opinion is quite convincing, it follows that Wogastisburg cannot have been the central seat of King Samo. Such a seat must have been deeper in the hinterland, must have been well fortified and must have had a central position in relation to the territory of the empire. The historian Ján Steinhübel considers the stronghold of Devín to be the most probable seat of Samo, or at least one of his several central seats. Compared with Carnuntum, which was already in decline by then, it indisputably had the advantage of being better protected against a sudden Avar incursion by the course of the Danube – and not only by it. The Roman emperor Valentinian, already mentioned above, had the stronghold fortified in 375 with an unusually high timber-and-earth rampart, which perfectly protected the castle hill against potential attackers from the eastern and north-eastern side. It is the same rampart that later served the Great Moravian hillfort and the medieval castle well, whose massiveness we can still follow today from the eastern gate towards the northern gate, and part of which on the northern side has been dismantled, and is still being dismantled, before the eyes of the heritage authorities by local inhabitants seeking to “extend” their own yards. Such too can be heritage care in Slovakia, and such the attitude of citizens to a historical monument of the highest importance. Sadly, Devín is not an isolated case."

The historian Michal Lutovský and Naďa Profantová took on an interesting task in their book Samova ríša (Samo's Empire). In it they describe what the hillfort of Wogastisburg and life on it might have looked like at the time of the famous battle. Among other things they write:

"Let us now attempt – with the help of our knowledge from archaeologically investigated hillforts – an approximate idea of what Wogastisburg might have looked like inside. In time of peace only a small military garrison probably lived at the hillfort. Like the inhabitants of the villages, its members too most often lived in houses partly sunk into the ground, that is, in semi-sunken buildings. Rather exceptionally there could also be dwellings built at ground level, either in the form of log cabins or of houses with walls formed – similarly as with the semi-sunken buildings – of wattle of thin rods between posts driven in around the perimeter of the structure. Such wattle was then covered with a clay layer – daub. Ground-level dwellings usually had a rectangular plan, as opposed to the square semi-sunken buildings, and tended to be somewhat more spacious. But they too most often consisted of a single room. In its centre we usually find an open hearth.

The cottages stood rather along the inner perimeter of the ramparts and so bordered a free central open space. In it there could have stood a princely or a magnate's palace, represented by a log structure of larger dimensions, divided most likely into two spaces – a larger antechamber and a main hall. From later periods we know such structures with a stone footing as well (for instance the princely palace at Mikulčice or at Libice), but we can hardly assume one for our period and for a hillfort that probably did not have central importance. The open space in the middle could, however, also have been completely free; a palace building need not have occurred at the hillfort at all.

The warriors were not the only group of inhabitants of the hillfort. Either directly in the enclosure of the hillfort itself or in the fortified bailey, craftsmen lived and worked. Among the semi-sunken buildings were interspersed smithies and the workshops of other craftsmen whose work was needed for the production and the maintenance of weapons and military equipment. In the more important centres the range of crafts widened; producers of luxury goods were added, especially metal casters, metal beaters and goldsmiths.

Life at the hillfort certainly also required many facilities of an economic character: stabling for the warriors' horses and for other livestock, facilities for storing grain and fodder. Of all that, however, we know very little. With more certainty we know only the underground grain stores – that is, grain pits – with a narrow neck. In these, however, it was advantageous to keep only grain for sowing, since frequent opening would have devalued their preservative capacity. We therefore have reason to assume the existence of other, above-ground types of granary as well, which archaeological excavation mostly cannot detect."
